name: Aaron Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have answered delivery and refund calls at the contact centre for thirteen years. I finished secondary school and know the ordinary claims well, though I still hand the odd fraud case to a specialist. The pay is low for the job. I use our approved AI search every day to find the rule, but the order record decides what I tell a customer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Grace serves meals at a school, and our children are grown and live on their own. We have less than a month of expenses saved and few similar centres nearby. I like getting a customer’s parcel back onto the right route. Retirement is in the distance, but I have not checked what money would come in if I stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the desk AI Plateau looks like the search box we already have. I would still read the order number aloud before promising a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the delivery calls remain, but Grace’s school-meal hours fall during breaks and we have less than a month saved. A small tool does not pay the electricity bill when her shifts stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep handling delivery claims and check each AI result against the actual order. In the first year of small change, I’d stop buying a sandwich on my two late shifts and keep that money for the next school break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about cash, not the search box. School holidays arrive whether the call queue is busy or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the AI search miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the search showed the return policy for the right item but the wrong order. I caught it from the delivery date before anyone issued a credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace (my partner) and I would pack food for those late shifts. I am not pretending two sandwiches will replace her wages; it gives us a little room.

say: I’d keep an **order-number check** before promising refunds.
I’d say **AI search** remains a shortcut beside the actual order.
think: I think **delivery calls** keep paying in this picture.
I worry **school-break hours** and thin savings make bills tight.
do: Keep **handling delivery claims** and verify AI results against original orders.
Skip **two late-shift sandwiches** weekly and keep the money for school breaks.
S0.quote: School holidays arrive whether the call queue is busy or not.
fieldNote: His **AI use** is daily but checked against original orders.
Grace’s **school-break hours** vary while savings are thin.
The **sandwich cut** is modest, not a replacement for lost wages.

steps.text: Keep handling delivery claims and check AI search against original orders
Skip two weekly late-shift sandwiches and hold the money for school breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will clear the easy parcel questions, and we should keep paid time for claims that come back wrong. I would ask management for the actual rota by shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my thirteen years should keep me on the harder calls, but one agent may be given more cases and fewer paid hours. We cannot bridge a long cut with our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the centre’s new AI return-checker during a paid demonstration and then use it on five old disputed orders with a coworker watching. If my shifts fall in the first year, I’d look at posted paid delivery-desk jobs nearby only where written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel; I would keep my current work until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, interested in whether the checker catches the right order. I can try a new tool without volunteering to lose a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which claim would test the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feed it an order with a replacement parcel and an old tracking number. If it picks the old route, an agent needs time to change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about a later finish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace (my partner) would compare the new rota with her school kitchen hours. A later finish may require a bus that no longer runs.

say: I’d request **paid rota hours** for disputed returns after easy parcel questions move.
I’d test **replacement parcels** against the new return checker.
think: I think my **thirteen years** may keep harder calls.
I fear **fewer hours** could cut my pay even when I handle more cases.
do: Learn **AI return checker** through paid demonstration and five supervised old orders.
Inspect **posted delivery work** after cuts only with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages and hours.
Check **Grace’s kitchen rota** against shift finish and last bus; keep paid calls until suitable offer signed.
feel: **Anxious** about shifts, willing to test a tool.
S1.quote: I can try a new tool without volunteering to lose a shift.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** includes five supervised cases, beyond daily rule search.
The **bus timetable** and Grace’s kitchen hours affect a new rota.
A move needs **written full-week net pay** and a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could route a parcel, decide a refund and answer the caller. Robots around 2031 are later; our calls could go before the loading bay changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my call hours might disappear in a short time. Grace’s school-meal pay and our few weeks saved would not meet every bill while I searched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for written cut dates and postpone replacing a still-working washing machine. If the calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d ask the local depot about a posted paid returns-counter vacancy and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel and a shift I can reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A washing machine can run one more year; our wages cannot disappear for one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the counter handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the counter actually handles returned parcels or only enters numbers. Thinking AI could do the numbers by 2028, while physical handling may change when robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace (my partner) would check the bus home from the depot. I would not pay for daily lifts out of the few weeks we have saved.

say: I’d ask for **written cut dates** on delivery calls.
I’d separate **2028 records work** from later physical robots.
think: I think **most call hours** might disappear quickly.
I know **thin savings** and school-meal pay cannot bridge a long search.
do: Defer **washing-machine replacement** while it works and seek written cut notice in 2026.
Inspect **posted paid depot counter** after call loss; move only on signed after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours and bus.
S2.quote: A washing machine can run one more year; our wages cannot disappear for one month.
fieldNote: The **appliance delay** is conditional on the machine working.
He distinguishes **thinking AI** from later hands-on robots.
Depot work needs **written net weekly pay** and a bus home.

steps.text: Delay replacing washing machine while it works
Inspect posted paid depot counter and move only on signed after-travel bill-covering wages/hours and bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to see a real depot job before I quit a call desk. I would tell coworkers not to buy a course merely because its name sounds safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my parcel knowledge could help me check physical returns, though AI will still do the records and robots around 2034 may later handle boxes. I want to learn from the person doing the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d ask for one supervised paid returns shift only if the depot has a posted paid vacancy and the lifting is safe for me. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only after a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare and a route home, keeping my call job until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to see the work. I would rather try one paid loading-bay morning than own a certificate for an absent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the paid shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a damaged box against its order note while a worker watches. If the load hurts my back, I would say so before agreeing to a rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the journey work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace (my partner) would look at the shift finish and the last bus. We need the wage after fare, not a rate that assumes I can drive there.

say: I’d seek a **supervised paid shift** for a posted depot opening.
I’d warn against **course adverts** with no actual job.
think: I think my **parcel knowledge** could help with returns.
I know **2034 robots** may later handle physical boxes.
do: Try **supervised paid depot work** only for posted vacancy with safe lifting.
Move after 2031 only on **signed after-fare bill-covering wages**, written hours and last bus; keep paid calls until then.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect real physical work.

fieldNote: He chooses a **paid practical shift**, not an invented course commitment.
Safe lifting is a **real personal gate** before accepting a rota.

steps.text: Try supervised paid depot shift only for posted paid vacancy with safe lifting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my desk AGI by 2036 gives us a long look at whether delivery calls stay paid. I would ask for the evening rota each year before I set a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need my call wage at 68; Grace and I have not checked what income would continue after work. Full thinking AI could take the calls in 2036, with robots around 2039 later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid delivery calls and compare our real income with bills before choosing any stop-work date. If I still need wages after 2036 and call hours fall, I’d seek posted paid work I can reach and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this year’s bills despite the long warning. A decade is not a cash reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which months would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Grace (my partner) to show me which months her kitchen work pays and what income is verified for later life. I would not assume a pension just because I turn 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own rent and plans. I would not put their earnings in our budget unless they offered help with a clear limit.

I’d say **2036 AGI** may still take delivery calls.

I cannot assume **retirement income** before checking it.
do: Keep **paid delivery calls** and request the evening rota yearly before deciding any stop-work date.
Compare **Grace’s paid kitchen months** and verified later-life income with bills before planning a work exit.
Seek **posted reachable work** only if wages remain needed after 2036 and calls fall; move on signed after-travel bill-covering terms.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills despite the decade.

fieldNote: His **thin savings** keep present bills tense even in 2036.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could do the delivery claims I have handled for years, and our small reserve would not bridge many lost shifts. I would need a clear date for cuts and a posted paid job I could reach without sacrificing the whole week’s wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: My father taught me to learn a trade by standing beside someone doing it. If I change work, give me a paid day on a real shift before selling me a certificate.

headlineQuote: If I change work, give me a paid day on a real shift before selling me a certificate.
portrait: At **58**, Aaron is an experienced mid-level delivery agent with secondary schooling and average skill.
He and Grace have **grown children**, low pay and less than a month of expenses saved.
He uses **AI search daily** and checks each original order record.
With **few nearby centres**, he seeks paid practical work before any job change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove delivery claims before he replaces his low wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut dates** and posted paid reachable work with full-week wages would help.
